body.text: On November 17, leaders of Quad member countries, India, Australia, the U.S. and Japan, met on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit in Manila.

The summit had several “firsts” to its credit. Not only was this the first time that a Quad summit was held in a non-Quad country – the Philippines hosted the meeting in its capacity as the current chair of ASEAN – it was also the first since U.S. President Donald Trump began his second term and Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae assumed office in October last year.

Importantly, the Quad summit in Manila happened after two years. New Delhi was due to host the leaders’ summit after India took over the chairmanship from the United States last year. But it never took place. This was reportedly because of Trump’s reluctance to travel to India. Over the past year, India-U.S. relations have faced much turbulence due to recurring economic and geopolitical frictions.

Despite some speculation that Modi and Trump would hold a bilateral meeting in Manila, that did not happen; Modi flew back to New Delhi soon after the summit. According to Indian news sources, a bilateral meeting is expected next month in Florida, on the margins of the G20 leaders’ summit. This is yet to be officially confirmed.

Several important initiatives were announced during the summit in Manila, including the inaugural Quad Business Leaders’ Forum that brings together business leaders, government officials and policy experts from the four countries to “foster greater business ties” across private sectors. The leaders also announced that their maritime patrol aircraft are scheduled to participate in an exercise for the first time in a Quad context. This is scheduled for 2027 in Mumbai.

The leaders welcomed the Indo-Pacific Maritime Surveillance Collaboration framework, which was launched in New Delhi in May 2026, following the Quad Foreign Ministers’ Meeting. This is aimed at stepping up information sharing and maritime domain awareness capacity in the region. Apart from this, the leaders also reiterated support for the AI Accelerator, a joint initiative announced during the Quad foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta last month, in addition to “enhanced” Quad Cybersecurity Cooperation.

Amidst concerns over the Indo-Pacific’s dwindling importance in Trump’s foreign policy prioritization, the Manila summit was a welcome development as far as political signaling on Washington’s commitment to the region is concerned. Ahead of the summit, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for Global Public Affairs Dylan Johnson took to X to dismiss reports of Quad “withering” under Trump as “utterly ridiculous.”
Addressing the summit, Trump praised how the Quad nations “represent some of the most important partnerships in the entire world” and are among the most successful.

Amid these deliverables, the summit in Manila did not reflect well for India’s chairship of the grouping. It is unclear who the official host of the meeting in Manila was, which, according to The Hindu’s diplomatic editor, Suhasini Haidar, was discussed during U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visits to India in May and October this year. Citing unnamed sources, Haidar said that New Delhi is unwilling to hand over the chairship of the summit without hosting a leaders-level meeting in the country. Australia is slated to chair the Quad in 2027. At the Manila summit, no mention was made of any leaders’ meeting for the next year.

Since the Quad’s upgradation in 2021, New Delhi has not hosted any leaders’ summit on its own soil. Hosting major international summits in India serves as a vital soft power signaling tool to project itself as a consequential diplomatic actor, as seen during the 2023 G20 Summit, the India AI Impact Summit 2026, and the 2026 BRICS Summit. The optics of hosting the Quad summit in a third country undercuts India’s standing as an agenda setter within the group.

Some have argued that hosting the summit in Manila was a matter of “convenience.” While this may hold some truth, it risks diluting the very optics of signaling the importance of the grouping and reflects ongoing coordination friction among members, undercutting the message that the Quad reflects some of the strongest partnerships in the world.

Experts have been quick to note that the pre-meeting photo-op in Manila reflected the “underlying friction and asymmetric power dynamics” currently defining the Quad. While Trump kept answering questions from the crowd solo, other Quad leaders stood beside him silently. Modi’s visible discomfort, with Trump’s hijacking of the routine summit photo-op into an impromptu press conference, where he tried unsuccessfully to get Trump to wrap up an exchange with reporters, also did not go unnoticed. This contrasts with the “easy camaraderie among equals,” which was visible during the early years of the Quad’s revival.

While hosting the summit in Manila gave New Delhi the opportunity to signal support for the Philippines amid heightened tensions between Manila and Beijing, the joint statement did not mention the 2016 Arbitral Award—unlike the 2024 Wilmington Declaration. The statement was silent on maritime disputes and refrained from condemning the illegal conduct of nations in the region. Strikingly, it was only the Japanese statement that explicitly mentioned the East China Sea and the South China Sea, in the context of the four nations aligning their “strategic perspectives.” No such mention was made in the statements released by India, the United States and Australia.

Similarly, while Tokyo notes leader-level discussions on North Korea, the Middle East, including the situation surrounding Iran, the other three Quad members were silent on these issues. Neither did the 2026 joint statement mention the need to protect and preserve navigational rights and freedoms in the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which were explicitly highlighted in the Quad joint release from the foreign ministers’ meeting on October 31. These raise important questions about the degree to which India, as chair, was able to set the agenda for the meeting.
Still, New Delhi did draw benefits from hosting the summit in Manila as it brought greater coherence to its regional diplomacy.

In his book “Act East to Act Indo-Pacific: India’s Expanding Neighbourhood,” Prabir De writes that under the Modi government, New Delhi’s “Act East” policy is transforming into “Act Indo-Pacific” while keeping Southeast Asia at the heart of its engagements. The fact that the Quad summit was held on the sidelines of an ASEAN summit indicates a certain degree of comfort among ASEAN countries towards the Quad. This is significant as ASEAN countries have traditionally been hesitant in engaging with the Quad due to fear of upsetting China.

Despite speculation about the Quad’s second demise after the leaders’ meeting did not take place in 2024, the group is moving forward. Regular foreign ministers’ meetings and engagements have taken place without interruption. Yet, if the leaders’ summit is largely about political signaling, hosting the meeting in a non-Quad country inadvertently highlights the challenges that India has faced as the chair of the summit.

If future Quad summits continue to be planned around Trump’s travel schedule, the grouping risks sending a costly signal to the world – that convenience rather than strategic convergence sets the group’s agenda.
